Seven linguistically motivated transformation rules (dropping conjunction, removing conjuncts, passivization, removing adjuncts, swapping relative clauses for participles, negation, and constrained mixing of dependents) can systematically generate semantically related, contradictory, and neutral sentence pairs for Polish

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a systematic procedure for constructing a Polish evaluation dataset (10K sentence pairs) for compositional distributional semantics (CDS) models, adapting the English SICK corpus methodology to account for morphological complexity, free word order, and resource scarcity. The logical argument structure is well-organized and generally coherent: (1) motivation and background establish why CDS evaluation datasets are needed for under-resourced languages; (2) the core methodological contribution describes seven linguistically motivated transformation rules and a two-stage annotation procedure; (3) empirical results report inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ=0.732 for entailment, α=0.780 for relatedness). The paper's reasoning chain is sound at the macro level—each section builds logically on prior sections—but exhibits critical gaps in evidence linking claims to outcomes, particularly regarding (a) whether the adapted procedure is truly generalizable beyond Polish, (b) whether the dataset has been validated through actual CDS model evaluation, and (c) whether the two-stage annotation procedure demonstrably improves quality relative to single-stage annotation. The paper conflates resource scarcity and linguistic structure as barriers to direct SICK adaptation without systematically isolating their relative contributions. Transformation rule productivity is highly uneven (2.0% to 26.8%), raising questions about whether underrepresented rules are linguistically rare or procedurally constrained. The paper's claim that the dataset is 'suitable' for CDS evaluation is inferred from agreement metrics rather than empirically demonstrated through actual model evaluation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a systematic procedure for constructing a Polish evaluation dataset (10K sentence pairs) for compositional distributional semantics (CDS) models, adapting the English SICK corpus methodology to account for Polish morphology, syntax, and resource constraints. The core contribution is methodological: demonstrating how to adapt SICK's design to a morphologically rich, under-resourced language through seven linguistically motivated transformation rules, a two-stage annotation procedure with human verification, and bidirectional entailment annotation. The paper reports inter-annotator agreement of κ=0.732 (Fleiss' kappa for entailment) and α=0.780 (Krippendorff's alpha for relatedness), claiming these metrics indicate dataset suitability for Polish CDS model evaluation. The work is well-documented and addresses a genuine gap in NLP resources for under-resourced languages. However, the methodology audit reveals critical gaps in reproducibility, validity assumptions, and empirical validation that must be resolved before the dataset's utility can be confidently assessed. The paper conflates resource scarcity with linguistic necessity, lacks quantitative evidence for key design choices, and makes suitability claims without empirical demonstration.

20 pairs with no majority label (X) not analyzed; impact on dataset reliability unclear; these pairs are excluded from analysis but represent 0.2% of data
Bidirectional annotation (each pair annotated in both directions) may inflate apparent agreement if annotators treat (a,b) and (b,a) similarly; no analysis of whether agreement is symmetric
No analysis of agreement by transformation type; some transformations may have lower agreement than others
No comparison of agreement metrics to SICK corpus; SICK uses different annotation procedure (10 ratings on Likert scale averaged, not 3 judges with majority voting)

identified_claims.claim_label: Dataset suitability for Polish CDS model evaluation
identified_claims.claim_text: The Polish dataset is suitable for evaluation of Polish compositional distributional semantics models
evidence: 10K sentence pairs with human annotations for relatedness and entailment
Inter-annotator agreement metrics reported (κ=0.732 for entailment, α=0.780 for relatedness)
Dataset will be made publicly available
Comparable structure to SICK corpus
uncertainty_flags: No empirical validation: dataset has not been used to evaluate actual Polish CDS models; suitability is inferred from agreement metrics, not demonstrated
No analysis of linguistic phenomenon coverage (e.g., which syntactic/semantic phenomena are well-represented, which are underrepresented)
No comparison of dataset characteristics (size, label distribution, phenomenon coverage) to SICK to assess true comparability
Suitability claim is inferred from agreement metrics but not directly demonstrated; high agreement does not necessarily imply suitability for model evaluation
No discussion of potential biases in dataset (e.g., image selection bias from 46 thematic groups, annotator bias from linguistically trained annotators)
No analysis of whether dataset covers phenomena relevant to real-world CDS applications
No discussion of dataset limitations or appropriate use cases

strengths.title: Addresses genuine resource gap for under-resourced languages
strengths.description: The paper tackles a real and important problem: the lack of evaluation datasets for CDS models in morphologically rich, under-resourced languages like Polish. This is a legitimate contribution to NLP infrastructure.
evidence: Polish is described as 'completely different than English in at least two dimensions' (fusional, free word order, under-resourced)
Availability of test data is argued to stimulate model development (Section 1.4)
Dataset will be made publicly available, enabling future research

strengths.title: Systematic documentation of adaptation procedure
strengths.description: The paper provides detailed, step-by-step documentation of the dataset construction procedure, including image selection, transformation rules, annotation guidelines, and quality checks. This level of detail supports reproducibility and provides a template for other languages.
evidence: Section 2.1 describes image selection and thematic grouping (46 groups, 1K images)
Section 2.2 provides detailed linguistic examples for each of seven transformation rules
Section 2.3 formally specifies the pairing procedure with mathematical notation
Section 3.1-3.3 document annotation assumptions, two-stage procedure, and post-corrections
Tables 1-3 provide quantitative summaries of transformations, relatedness, and entailment distributions

strengths.title: Linguistically principled transformation rules
strengths.description: The seven transformation rules are linguistically motivated and tailored to Polish morphosyntax. The rules address phenomena specific to fusional languages (passivization, participle constructions, negation) rather than applying English-centric transformations.
evidence: Rules include Polish-specific constructions: active adjectival participles, contemporary adverbial participles, relative clause-participle swapping
Examples provided for each rule show linguistic sophistication (e.g., Odpoczywający rowerzysta obserwuje morze)
Rules target different semantic relations: similarity (rules 1-5), contradiction (rule 6), neutrality (rule 7)
All transformations performed on dependency structures, respecting syntactic structure

strengths.title: Two-stage annotation procedure with quality control
strengths.description: The introduction of leader judges to verify and correct automatically transformed sentences before annotation is a pragmatic quality control measure that acknowledges the error-proneness of automatic transformations based on imperfect parsing.
evidence: Leader judges correct incomprehensible and ungrammatical sentences with minimal changes (Section 3.2)
Post-correction process captures annotator feedback: 228 sentences corrected for punctuation/typos, 141 for more significant changes (Section 3.3)
Procedure explicitly designed to avoid annotating erroneous sentences
Two-stage procedure is documented and could be replicated for other languages

strengths.title: Appropriate statistical measures for inter-annotator agreement
strengths.description: The paper uses Fleiss' kappa for categorical entailment labels and Krippendorff's alpha for ordinal relatedness scores, which are appropriate choices for multiple raters and different measurement scales.
evidence: Fleiss' kappa chosen for entailment because: (1) more than two raters, (2) categorical labels, (3) different items can be rated by different judges (Section 4.2)
Krippendorff's α chosen for relatedness because: (1) multiple judges, (2) different magnitudes of disagreement, (3) missing values possible, (4) ordinal measurement appropriate (Section 4.2)
Authors acknowledge limitations of Fleiss' kappa for relatedness (κ=0.336 for 6-point scale, κ=0.543 for 3-point scale) and justify switch to Krippendorff's α

strengths.title: Bidirectional entailment annotation reflects non-symmetric nature of entailment
strengths.description: The paper correctly recognizes that entailment is non-symmetric and implements bidirectional annotation, where each pair (a,b) is annotated for entailment in both directions. This is linguistically principled and differs from SICK's approach.
evidence: Section 2.3 states: 'an entailment relation between two sentences must not be symmetric'
For each sentence pair (a,b), its reverse (b,a) is also included in corpus (Section 2.3)
Each sentence pair is annotated for entailment in both directions (Section 3.2)
Final entailment labels are pairs: entailment+neutral, contradiction+neutral, entailment+entailment, etc. (Table 3)

strengths.title: Reasonable dataset size and label distribution
strengths.description: The final dataset of 10K sentence pairs is a substantial resource comparable to SICK (also 10K pairs). The label distribution shows reasonable coverage of different semantic relations, with majority of pairs being neutral+neutral (6477) and entailment+neutral (1741).
evidence: Final dataset: 10K sentence pairs (20K ordered pairs due to bidirectionality)

Label distribution (Table 3): neutral+neutral 6477 (64.8%), entailment+neutral 1741 (17.4%), entailment+entailment 932 (9.3%), contradiction+contradiction 717 (7.2%), contradiction+neutral 113 (1.1%), X 20 (0.2%)
Relatedness distribution (Table 2) shows spread across 0-5 scale, with concentration in middle ranges (3-4)

concerns.title: Lack of empirical validation that dataset enables meaningful CDS model evaluation
concerns.description: The paper claims the dataset is 'suitable for evaluating Polish CDS models' but provides no empirical evidence. No Polish CDS models have been evaluated on this dataset; suitability is inferred from inter-annotator agreement metrics alone. This is a critical gap between claimed utility and demonstrated utility.
evidence: Abstract claims dataset 'may be used for evaluation of compositional distributional semantics models of Polish'
Section 4.2 concludes 'our dataset is a reliable resource for purpose of evaluating compositional distributional semantics model of Polish' based solely on agreement metrics
No section describes evaluation of actual CDS models on the dataset
No analysis of whether dataset covers phenomena relevant to CDS model evaluation
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (1) evaluate at least one Polish CDS model on the dataset and report results, or (2) revise claims to state that dataset 'is intended for' or 'could be used for' evaluation rather than claiming it 'is suitable for' evaluation. Alternatively, provide detailed analysis of phenomenon coverage and comparison to SICK to support suitability claim.

concerns.title: No quantification of dependency parsing errors and their impact on transformation quality
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges that transformations are 'fully automatic and to a certain extent based on imperfect dependency parsing' but provides no quantification of parsing error rates or analysis of how parsing errors propagate to transformed sentences. This is critical because transformation quality depends on parsing accuracy.
evidence: Section 3.2 states: 'Since the transformation process is fully automatic and to a certain extent based on imperfect dependency parsing, we cannot ignore errors in the transformed sentences'
No error analysis provided for the dependency parser (Wróblewska, 2014)
No quantification of how many transformed sentences contain parsing-induced errors
Two-stage annotation with leader judges is introduced to mitigate errors, but no analysis of error detection rate
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct error analysis on a sample of transformed sentences: (1) manually evaluate parsing accuracy on original sentences, (2) analyze how parsing errors affect transformation quality, (3) quantify error detection rate by leader judges. Report these metrics in the paper.

concerns.title: Uneven transformation productivity raises questions about rule completeness and applicability
concerns.description: The seven transformation rules show highly uneven productivity (2.0% for dropping conjunction to 26.8% for mixing dependents). This raises questions about whether underrepresented rules are truly unproductive in Polish or whether the procedure limits their application. No analysis of why some rules are so rare.
evidence: Table 1 shows distribution: dropping conjunction 2.0%, removing conjunct 6.9%, passivisation 12.8%, removing adjuncts 14.5%, swapping rc↔ptcp 18.4%, negation 18.6%, mixing dependents 26.8%
No analysis of why dropping conjunction is so rare (2.0%)
No discussion of whether rare rules should be weighted differently or excluded
No comparison of transformation distribution to SICK expansion methodology
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze why certain transformations are rare: (1) are they linguistically rare in Polish? (2) are they procedurally limited (e.g., few sentences with coordinated predicates)? (3) should the procedure be modified to increase coverage of rare rules? Provide analysis and justify final rule set.

concerns.title: No comparison of inter-annotator agreement metrics to SICK or other semantic datasets
concerns.description: The paper claims inter-annotator agreement is 'quite satisfactory' (κ=0.732 for entailment, α=0.780 for relatedness) but provides no benchmark. What constitutes 'satisfactory' is field-dependent and depends on the task. No comparison to SICK agreement scores or other semantic evaluation datasets.
evidence: Section 4.2 states: 'there is inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.732 for entailment labels in Polish evaluation dataset, which is quite satisfactory as for a semantic labelling task'
No reference to SICK agreement scores
No comparison to other semantic relatedness datasets (e.g., SemEval tasks)
No justification for what constitutes 'satisfactory' agreement for semantic tasks
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide comparison of agreement metrics to: (1) SICK corpus agreement scores (if available), (2) other semantic relatedness datasets, (3) published benchmarks for semantic annotation tasks. Discuss whether Polish agreement metrics are comparable to or different from English SICK.

concerns.title: Ordinal vs. interval measurement choice for Krippendorff's alpha not fully justified
concerns.description: The paper uses Krippendorff's α with ordinal measurement (α=0.780) for relatedness scores but notes that interval measurement gives higher α=0.785. The choice of ordinal is justified by doubt about meaningfulness of interval distances, but this doubt is not formally justified. The choice affects interpretation of agreement.
evidence: Section 4.2 states: 'We also test interval measurement, in which the distance between the attributes does have meaning and an average of an interval variable is computed. The interval score measured for relatedness annotations is quite high α = 0.785, but we doubt whether the distance between relatedness scores is meaningful in this case.'
No formal justification for why interval distances are not meaningful
Choice of ordinal vs. interval affects interpretation: α=0.780 (ordinal) vs. α=0.785 (interval)
No discussion of how this choice affects comparability to other datasets
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide formal justification for ordinal vs. interval measurement choice. Consider: (1) are relatedness scores truly ordinal (rank-ordered) or interval (equal distances)? (2) how does this choice affect comparability to SICK? (3) report both metrics and discuss implications. Alternatively, justify why ordinal is more appropriate for this task.

concerns.title: Twenty pairs with no majority entailment label (X) not analyzed
concerns.description: The dataset contains 20 pairs (0.2%) with no majority entailment label. These pairs are excluded from analysis but their existence raises questions about annotation reliability and how they should be handled. No analysis of why these pairs lack majority labels or what they represent.
evidence: Table 3 shows X label for 20 pairs (0.2% of 10K)
No analysis of these pairs in the paper
No discussion of how to handle pairs with no majority label
No analysis of whether these pairs represent genuine disagreement or annotation errors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze the 20 pairs with no majority label: (1) what are the annotation patterns (e.g., 1-1-1 split)? (2) do they represent genuine disagreement or annotation errors? (3) should they be excluded, re-annotated, or handled differently? Provide analysis and justify final handling.

concerns.title: Bidirectional annotation may inflate apparent agreement if annotators treat (a,b) and (b,a) symmetrically
concerns.description: The paper annotates each pair (a,b) in both directions (b,a). If annotators treat these as related decisions (e.g., if they see both versions), apparent agreement could be inflated. No analysis of whether agreement is symmetric or whether bidirectionality introduces bias.
evidence: Section 2.3 states: 'For each sentence pair (a,b) created according to this procedure, its reverse (b,a) is also included in our corpus'

Section 3.2 states: 'For each of the 1K images, the following 10 pairs are constructed... For each sentence pair (a,b) created according to this procedure, its reverse (b,a) is also included in our corpus'
No analysis of whether annotators see both (a,b) and (b,a) or whether they are annotated independently
No analysis of agreement symmetry (is agreement for (a,b) same as for (b,a)?)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze bidirectional annotation: (1) are (a,b) and (b,a) annotated independently or do annotators see both? (2) is agreement symmetric? (3) if not independent, does this inflate apparent agreement? Report agreement separately for (a,b) and (b,a) pairs to assess symmetry.

concerns.title: Post-correction procedure appears ad-hoc without systematic criteria
concerns.description: The paper describes post-corrections (228 sentences for punctuation/typos, 141 for more significant changes) but provides no systematic criteria for what constitutes a valid correction or how corrections were validated. The process appears ad-hoc and could introduce inconsistency.
evidence: Section 3.3 states: 'We thus decided to garner annotators' comments and suggestions for improving sentences. After validation of these suggestions by an experienced linguist, it turns out that most of these proposals concern punctuation errors and typos in 228 distinct sentences'
No specification of what constitutes a valid correction
No inter-rater agreement on correction validity
No analysis of whether corrections changed semantic content
No discussion of how re-annotation was conducted for 141 modified pairs
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Document the post-correction procedure: (1) specify systematic criteria for valid corrections, (2) report inter-rater agreement on correction validity, (3) analyze whether corrections changed semantic content, (4) describe re-annotation procedure for modified pairs. Alternatively, justify why ad-hoc corrections are acceptable.

concerns.title: No inter-annotator agreement analysis between leader judges and other judges
concerns.description: The two-stage procedure relies on leader judges to verify and correct transformed sentences. However, no inter-annotator agreement is measured between leader judges and other judges to assess whether verification is effective or whether leader corrections introduce bias.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes two-stage procedure: leader judges verify and correct, then other judges annotate
No inter-rater agreement reported between leader judges and other judges
No analysis of whether leader corrections improve annotation quality
No comparison of agreement for pairs with vs. without leader corrections
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Measure inter-annotator agreement between leader judges and other judges: (1) do leader corrections improve agreement? (2) is there agreement between leader judges on what constitutes an error? (3) do leader corrections introduce systematic bias? Report these metrics to validate the two-stage procedure.

concerns.title: Conflation of resource scarcity and linguistic necessity in justifying adaptations
concerns.description: The paper conflates two distinct problems: (1) unavailability of Polish equivalents to ImageFlickr and SemEval datasets (resource scarcity) and (2) linguistic differences in Polish morphology and syntax (linguistic necessity). It's unclear which is the primary barrier to direct SICK adaptation or whether both are necessary.
evidence: Section 1.4 states: 'the implementation of particular building steps significantly differs from the original SICK design assumptions, which is caused by both lack of necessary extraneous resources for Polish (see Section 2.1) and demand for Polish-specific transformation rules (see Section 2.2)'
Section 2.1 addresses resource scarcity: 'Since we are not aware of accessibility of analogous resources for Polish, we have to select images first and then describe the selected images'

Section 2.2 addresses linguistic necessity: 'the expansion step, in turn, is implemented and the sentences provided by the authors are lexically and syntactically transformed in order to obtain derivative sentences'
No systematic analysis of which adaptations are due to resource scarcity vs. linguistic necessity
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Separate resource-driven adaptations from linguistically-driven adaptations: (1) which adaptations would be necessary even with Polish ImageFlickr and SemEval data? (2) which adaptations are specific to Polish morphosyntax vs. general to fusional languages? (3) which adaptations could be avoided with more resources? This analysis would clarify generalizability to other languages.

concerns.title: No analysis of linguistic phenomenon coverage in dataset
concerns.description: The paper provides no analysis of which linguistic phenomena are well-represented in the dataset and which are underrepresented. This is critical for assessing whether the dataset is suitable for evaluating CDS models, which should handle diverse phenomena.
evidence: No section analyzes phenomenon coverage (e.g., which syntactic/semantic phenomena are represented)
No analysis of whether image-based descriptions capture phenomena relevant to CDS evaluation
No discussion of potential biases in phenomenon coverage (e.g., 46 thematic groups may not represent balanced coverage)
No comparison of phenomenon coverage to SICK
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze phenomenon coverage: (1) categorize sentence pairs by linguistic phenomena (e.g., negation, passivization, coordination, modification), (2) report distribution of phenomena, (3) identify underrepresented phenomena, (4) compare to SICK phenomenon coverage. This analysis would support claims about dataset suitability.

concerns.title: Annotator expertise (mostly linguists) may bias annotations toward linguistically sophisticated interpretations
concerns.description: The annotation team consists primarily of linguists (5 PhDs, 5 PhD students, 1 graduate, 1 undergraduate). This expertise may bias annotations toward linguistically sophisticated interpretations that don't generalize to non-expert annotators or native speakers without linguistic training.
evidence: Section 3.2 footnote 2 states: 'Our annotators have relatively strong linguistic background. Five of them have PhD in linguistics, five are PhD students, one is a graduate, and one is an undergraduate.'
No discussion of potential bias from linguistic expertise
No comparison of annotations from linguists vs. non-experts
No analysis of whether agreement would be different with non-expert annotators
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss potential bias from annotator expertise: (1) are linguistically trained annotators more likely to make certain judgments? (2) would non-expert annotators produce different annotations? (3) is this bias acceptable for a CDS evaluation dataset? Alternatively, conduct validation with non-expert annotators to assess generalizability.

concerns.title: Generalizability claims about applicability to other fusional languages not empirically supported
concerns.description: The paper claims the procedure is applicable to other morphologically rich or under-resourced languages, but this is demonstrated only for Polish. No evidence that the procedure generalizes to other fusional languages with different morphosyntactic properties.
evidence: Abstract states: 'The designed procedure is verified on Polish, a fusional language with a relatively free word order'
Section 1.4 states: 'We start with a high-quality dataset for Polish, which is a completely different language than English in at least two dimensions'
No testing on other languages
No discussion of which aspects of the procedure are Polish-specific vs. generalizable
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify generalizability: (1) which aspects of the procedure are specific to Polish? (2) which aspects would generalize to other fusional languages? (3) what modifications would be needed for other languages? Alternatively, revise claims to state that procedure is 'demonstrated for Polish' rather than 'applicable to other languages'.

concerns.title: No validation that transformation rules preserve compositionality principle
concerns.description: The paper claims transformations are designed to produce semantically related, contradictory, or neutral pairs, but provides no independent validation that transformations preserve the compositionality principle. Semantic validity of transformed sentences is not verified.
evidence: Section 2.2 states: 'The first five transformations are designed to produce sentences with a similar meaning, the sixth transformation outputs sentences with a contradictory meaning, and the seventh transformation should generate sentences with a neutral (or unrelated) meaning'
No independent validation of semantic validity
No inter-rater agreement on whether transformations produce intended semantic relations
Two-stage annotation with leader judges checks for grammaticality but not semantic validity
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate transformation rules: (1) conduct manual evaluation of a sample of transformed sentences to verify they produce intended semantic relations, (2) measure inter-rater agreement on semantic validity, (3) analyze error rates by transformation type. This validation would support claims about transformation quality.

concerns.title: Image selection bias not discussed; 46 thematic groups may not represent balanced phenomenon coverage
concerns.description: The paper selects 1K images from 8K ImageFlickr dataset and organizes them into 46 thematic groups with highly uneven distribution (6 to 94 images per group). This selection process may introduce bias in phenomenon coverage, but no analysis is provided.
evidence: Section 2.1 states: 'we independently extract 1K images and split them into 46 thematic groups (e.g. children, musical instruments, motor-bikes, football, dogs). Numbers of images within individual thematic groups vary from 6 images in the volleyball and telephoning groups to 94 images in the various people group'
No analysis of whether 46 thematic groups represent balanced phenomenon coverage
No discussion of selection criteria for 1K images
No analysis of potential biases in image selection
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze image selection bias: (1) what criteria were used to select 1K images from 8K? (2) are 46 thematic groups representative of linguistic phenomena? (3) does uneven distribution (6-94 images per group) introduce bias? (4) how does image selection affect phenomenon coverage? Provide analysis or justify selection procedure.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct methodological precedent; this paper adapts SICK methodology to Polish
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SIMILARITY: Both construct 10K sentence pairs annotated for semantic relatedness and entailment. DIFFERENCE: SICK uses English sentences from ImageFlickr and SemEval datasets; Polish dataset uses independently selected images and Polish-specific transformations. SICK uses 10 Likert ratings averaged; Polish uses 3 judges with majority voting for entailment and Krippendorff's alpha for relatedness.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved from external literature corpus; referenced extensively in paper (Bentivogli et al., 2014)

comparable_works.relevance: Established evaluation framework for CDS models using SICK corpus
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SIMILARITY: Both evaluate CDS models on semantic relatedness and entailment. DIFFERENCE: SemEval task uses SICK corpus; Polish dataset is new resource for Polish CDS evaluation. No direct comparison of evaluation results.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in paper (Marelli et al., 2014); described as 'SemEval-2014 Shared Task 1' in Section 1.2

comparable_works.citation_label: Bruni et al. (2014) - Multimodal Distributional Semantics
comparable_works.relevance: Provides theoretical background on distributional semantics and semantic space models
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SIMILARITY: Both address distributional semantics and semantic relatedness. DIFFERENCE: Bruni et al. focus on multimodal semantics (text + image); Polish paper focuses on compositional semantics of sentences. No direct methodological overlap.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved from external literature corpus; relevant to distributional semantics background

uncertainty_flags: No empirical validation that dataset enables meaningful CDS model evaluation; suitability is inferred from agreement metrics alone
Dependency parsing quality not quantified; impact on transformation accuracy unknown
Transformation productivity highly uneven (2.0% to 26.8%); unclear if underrepresented rules are linguistically rare or procedurally limited
No comparison of inter-annotator agreement metrics to SICK or other semantic datasets; 'satisfactory' agreement not benchmarked
Ordinal vs. interval measurement choice for Krippendorff's α affects interpretation; choice not fully justified
Twenty pairs with no majority entailment label (X) not analyzed; impact on dataset reliability unclear
Bidirectional annotation may inflate apparent agreement if annotators treat (a,b) and (b,a) as related decisions; no analysis of symmetry
Post-correction procedure appears ad-hoc without systematic criteria; unclear if corrections introduced inconsistency
No inter-annotator agreement measured between leader judges and other judges to assess verification effectiveness
Annotator expertise (mostly linguists) may bias annotations; generalizability to non-expert annotators unknown
Generalizability to other fusional languages not tested; claims about applicability are speculative
No validation that transformation rules preserve compositionality principle; semantic validity of transformed sentences not independently verified
Image selection bias not discussed; 46 thematic groups may not represent balanced phenomenon coverage
No analysis of which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented in dataset
Conflation of resource scarcity and linguistic necessity in justifying adaptations; unclear which is primary barrier
alternative_interpretations: The two-stage annotation procedure may not improve quality for Polish specifically but rather for any language with imperfect automatic transformations. The claim about morphologically complex languages may be overgeneralized.

The uneven transformation productivity (2.0% to 26.8%) may reflect genuine linguistic properties of Polish (e.g., coordinated predicates are rare) rather than procedural limitations. Alternatively, it may reflect that some transformations are more useful for CDS evaluation than others.

The inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ=0.732 for entailment, α=0.780 for relatedness) may be satisfactory for Polish-specific reasons (e.g., linguistic ambiguity in Polish) rather than being generally satisfactory for semantic tasks. Comparison to SICK would clarify this.

The dataset may be suitable for evaluating Polish CDS models even without empirical validation, if the agreement metrics are comparable to SICK. The paper's inference from agreement to suitability may be reasonable if SICK's agreement metrics are similar.

The bidirectional annotation may not inflate agreement if annotators treat (a,b) and (b,a) as independent decisions. The paper's concern about symmetry may be unfounded if annotation procedure ensures independence.
The post-correction procedure may be acceptable as ad-hoc if the corrections are minor (228 punctuation/typos vs. 141 significant changes). The impact on dataset quality may be negligible.

The linguistic expertise of annotators may be appropriate for CDS evaluation, which requires sophisticated understanding of semantic relations. Non-expert annotators might produce less reliable annotations.
transparency_notes: This review is based on the paper text and shared extraction stage; no access to the actual dataset or annotation guidelines beyond what is described in the paper
The review focuses on methodological soundness and reproducibility, not on the novelty or significance of the contribution
Comparisons to SICK are limited because SICK agreement metrics are not provided in the paper; this is a significant gap
The review identifies major gaps in empirical validation (e.g., no evaluation of actual CDS models) that prevent full assessment of dataset utility
Some concerns (e.g., image selection bias, annotator expertise bias) are flagged as potential issues but may not be critical depending on the intended use case
The review acknowledges that the paper makes a genuine contribution to NLP infrastructure for under-resourced languages, despite methodological gaps

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper adapts an existing methodology (SICK) to a new language (Polish) with language-specific modifications. This is a methodological adaptation rather than a novel methodology. The innovation is in the specific transformation rules and annotation procedure for Polish, not in the overall approach. The contribution is primarily a resource (dataset) rather than a methodological innovation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper empirically validated the dataset by evaluating actual Polish CDS models and showing that the dataset enables meaningful model evaluation, the suitability claim would be much stronger
If the paper provided detailed comparison of Polish dataset characteristics (agreement metrics, phenomenon coverage, label distribution) to SICK, the comparability claim would be more credible
If the paper quantified dependency parsing errors and analyzed their impact on transformation quality, the reliability of the transformation procedure would be better established
If the paper tested the procedure on at least one other fusional language, the generalizability claim would be empirically supported
If the paper provided inter-annotator agreement analysis between leader judges and other judges, the effectiveness of the two-stage verification procedure would be demonstrated
If the paper analyzed phenomenon coverage and identified which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented, the dataset's suitability for CDS evaluation would be better justified

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes a genuine contribution to NLP infrastructure by providing a Polish evaluation dataset for CDS models, with systematic documentation of the construction procedure. However, major methodological gaps significantly limit confidence in the dataset's utility and reliability. The lack of empirical validation (no evaluation of actual CDS models), absence of quantified parsing error analysis, and missing comparisons to SICK are critical weaknesses. The inter-annotator agreement metrics are reasonable but not benchmarked against comparable datasets. The paper would be substantially strengthened by: (1) evaluating actual Polish CDS models on the dataset, (2) quantifying parsing errors and their impact, (3) comparing agreement metrics to SICK, (4) analyzing phenomenon coverage, and (5) validating transformation rules. The confidence interval reflects moderate-to-good quality for a resource paper with significant methodological gaps that prevent full assessment of utility.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a methodological adaptation of the SICK corpus construction procedure to Polish, a morphologically rich, under-resourced language with free word order. The core novelty claim is that SICK's methodology can be adapted to non-English languages through language-specific modifications, particularly: (1) alternative image selection and description procedures due to resource unavailability, (2) seven linguistically motivated transformation rules tailored to Polish morphosyntax, (3) a two-stage annotation procedure with human verification of automatically transformed sentences, and (4) bidirectional entailment annotation to handle non-symmetric relations. The contribution is fundamentally incremental—it extends an existing paradigm (SICK) to a new language context—but claims meaningful methodological innovation through linguistic adaptation. The paper's novelty resides in the systematic documentation of adaptation challenges and solutions rather than in fundamentally new theoretical insights or algorithmic innovations. The work is positioned as a resource contribution with methodological documentation, targeting under-resourced language communities. Key tension: the paper claims the procedure is 'comparable' to SICK and potentially generalizable to other fusional languages, yet provides no empirical validation of either claim, and the seven transformation rules appear highly Polish-specific rather than broadly applicable.

alternative_interpretations: The seven transformation rules may be Polish-specific rather than generalizable to other fusional languages. Different fusional languages (Hungarian, Finnish, Czech) have different morphosyntactic properties that may require different transformation rules. The claim about generalizability may be overstated.

The two-stage annotation procedure may not be necessary for Polish specifically but rather beneficial for any language with imperfect dependency parsing. The paper frames it as a Polish-specific solution, but it may be a general solution to automatic transformation errors.

The uneven transformation productivity (2.0% to 26.8%) may reflect the actual linguistic distribution in Polish rather than procedural limitations. Dropping conjunction may genuinely be rare in Polish descriptions of images, while mixing dependents may be common. This would not be a flaw but rather an accurate reflection of Polish linguistic properties.

The low Fleiss' kappa for relatedness (κ=0.336-0.543) may indicate that relatedness is genuinely difficult to annotate consistently, rather than a problem with the dataset. The switch to Krippendorff's α may be appropriate if ordinal measurement better captures the nature of disagreement.

The 20 pairs with no majority entailment label (X) may represent genuinely ambiguous cases where multiple interpretations are valid. Rather than a flaw, these may be valuable for understanding the limits of entailment annotation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This manuscript presents a dataset resource (10K Polish sentence pairs) and accompanying methodological procedure for constructing evaluation corpora for compositional distributional semantics (CDS) models in morphologically rich, under-resourced languages. The work adapts the SICK corpus methodology to Polish, a fusional language with free word order, introducing seven linguistically motivated transformation rules and a two-stage annotation procedure. From a disruptive-novelty lens, the contribution occupies an interesting but constrained conceptual space: the core innovation—adapting SICK to non-English languages with language-specific linguistic phenomena—is conceptually sound and addresses a genuine resource gap, yet the execution is primarily engineering-focused rather than introducing a fundamentally new evaluation paradigm. The paper demonstrates that direct SICK adaptation is insufficient for morphologically complex languages, but the proposed solution (seven transformation rules + two-stage annotation) is presented as pragmatic workaround rather than a principled reconceptualization of semantic evaluation. The work's disruptive potential lies in its implicit argument that language-specific evaluation methodologies are necessary, but this argument remains largely implicit and underexplored. The paper would benefit from more explicit theorization of *why* compositional semantics evaluation must diverge across language types, and whether the seven transformation rules represent a language-universal principle or Polish-specific engineering.

transparency_notes: This review applies a disruptive-novelty lens, which prioritizes identification of conceptually novel contributions that diverge from mainstream approaches. From this lens, the paper's contribution is primarily pragmatic adaptation rather than conceptual innovation.
The paper's strengths lie in practical resource contribution and transparent methodology documentation. Its weaknesses lie in limited conceptual novelty and unsupported generalizability claims.

The reviewer acknowledges that resource papers may have different novelty standards than methodological or theoretical papers. A resource contribution is valuable if it addresses a genuine gap and is of high quality, even if methodologically conventional.

The paper's claim that 'direct SICK adaptation is insufficient for fusional languages' is interesting but underdeveloped. The paper does not explain *why* fusional morphology and free word order necessitate different evaluation methodology, only that they require different transformation rules and resource selection.

The seven transformation rules are linguistically motivated but appear ad-hoc rather than derived from principled linguistic theory. A stronger contribution would derive these rules from linguistic typology or propose a framework for generating rules for any language.

The paper's generalizability claims are speculative. The authors assert that the procedure 'can be adapted' to other languages but provide no evidence. This is a common pattern in resource papers, but it weakens the novelty claim.

The two-stage annotation procedure is pragmatic but not novel. Similar quality-control mechanisms have been used in other annotation projects. The paper does not demonstrate that this procedure is necessary or superior for morphologically complex languages.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a Polish evaluation dataset (10K sentence pairs) for compositional distributional semantics models, adapting the SICK corpus methodology to account for morphological complexity and resource scarcity. The core claims are: (1) SICK methodology can be adapted to non-English languages; (2) direct adaptation is insufficient for fusional languages; (3) seven linguistically motivated transformation rules systematically generate semantic relations; (4) two-stage annotation improves quality; (5) inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ=0.732, α=0.780) indicate dataset suitability. As a claim verifier, I assess these claims against manuscript evidence and prior work. The paper provides systematic documentation and reasonable agreement metrics, but critical claims lack empirical support or benchmarking. The claim that the dataset is 'suitable' for CDS evaluation is inferred from agreement metrics rather than demonstrated through actual model evaluation. Transformation rule productivity is highly uneven (2.0%–26.8%), raising questions about completeness. The paper conflates resource scarcity and linguistic necessity without isolating their contributions. Comparability to SICK is asserted but not formally demonstrated. The two-stage annotation procedure is presented as improving quality, but no empirical comparison to single-stage annotation is provided. Generalizability claims to other fusional languages are speculative based on a single Polish case study.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: CDS evaluation datasets exist for English (SICK corpus) but not for under-resourced languages like Polish.
Premise 2: Availability of test data stimulates development of NLP tools and models.
Conclusion 1: Building a Polish CDS evaluation dataset will encourage Polish CDS model development.
Premise 3: SICK methodology is based on image descriptions and systematic transformations.
Premise 4: Polish is morphologically complex and has free word order, unlike English.
Premise 5: Polish lacks equivalent resources to ImageFlickr and SemEval datasets.
Conclusion 2: Direct SICK adaptation is insufficient; language-specific modifications are necessary.
Premise 6: Seven transformation rules can be designed to generate semantically related, contradictory, and neutral sentence pairs.
Premise 7: Two-stage annotation with human verification of transformed sentences improves quality.
Conclusion 3: A Polish dataset of 10K pairs with inter-annotator agreement κ=0.732 (entailment) and α=0.780 (relatedness) is suitable for CDS model evaluation.
Unstated assumption: Inter-annotator agreement metrics alone are sufficient to establish dataset suitability without empirical validation through actual model evaluation.
Unstated assumption: Transformation rule productivity distribution (2.0%–26.8%) reflects linguistic properties rather than procedural limitations.
Unstated assumption: Two-stage annotation demonstrably improves quality relative to single-stage annotation (no baseline comparison provided).

Inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ=0.732 for entailment via Fleiss' kappa; α=0.780 for relatedness via Krippendorff's alpha) are in a reasonable range for semantic annotation tasks, suggesting consistent annotation procedures.

The paper provides systematic, reproducible documentation of the adaptation procedure, including image selection, transformation rules, pairing procedures, and annotation protocols—valuable for researchers attempting similar adaptations for other languages.

The two-stage annotation procedure with leader judge verification is a pragmatic quality-control mechanism that acknowledges the error-proneness of automatic transformations based on imperfect dependency parsing.
The paper transparently acknowledges deviations from SICK methodology and explains the rationale for each deviation, supporting reproducibility and enabling assessment of adaptation necessity.
Bidirectional entailment annotation (annotating both (a,b) and (b,a) pairs) is linguistically principled and appropriately handles the non-symmetric nature of entailment relations.

All reviewers flag this as a critical gap affecting dataset reliability.

Empirical validation of dataset suitability: The paper claims the dataset is 'suitable for evaluating Polish CDS models' but has not been used to evaluate actual Polish CDS models. All reviewers identify this as a critical gap between claimed utility and demonstrated utility.

meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a valuable resource contribution (Polish CDS evaluation dataset) with systematic documentation and reasonable inter-annotator agreement metrics. However, it makes several claims that lack empirical support: (1) dataset suitability for CDS model evaluation is inferred from agreement metrics rather than demonstrated through actual model evaluation; (2) two-stage annotation improvement is asserted without empirical comparison to single-stage baseline; (3) generalizability to other fusional languages is claimed without cross-linguistic validation; (4) comparability to SICK is asserted without formal comparison of dataset characteristics. The paper would be significantly strengthened by addressing these gaps. Minimum revisions should include: (a) qualifying generalizability claims to reflect that procedure is 'demonstrated for Polish' rather than 'applicable to other languages,' (b) revising suitability claim to state dataset 'is designed for' or 'has potential for' CDS evaluation rather than claiming it 'is suitable for' without empirical demonstration, (c) providing SICK agreement scores for comparison if available in literature. Recommended revisions should include: (d) quantifying dependency parsing quality and analyzing impact on transformation accuracy, (e) analyzing transformation rule productivity distribution to explain why some rules are underrepresented, (f) providing empirical comparison of two-stage vs. single-stage annotation on a subset of data, (g) analyzing linguistic phenomenon coverage and comparing to SICK. The paper's core contribution (Polish dataset) is valuable and publication-worthy, but claims should be calibrated to match evidence. The resource itself addresses a genuine gap and will likely be useful for Polish NLP community regardless of whether all methodological claims are fully supported.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a solid practical contribution by providing the first large-scale Polish evaluation dataset for CDS models. The systematic documentation of the adaptation procedure is valuable for other researchers. However, several of your key claims require stronger empirical support. Specific recommendations: (1) Revise abstract and conclusions to qualify generalizability claims—state that procedure 'has been demonstrated for Polish' rather than claiming it 'can be adapted to non-English languages' without evidence. (2) Revise suitability claim in Section 4.2—either evaluate actual Polish CDS models on the dataset, or state that dataset 'is designed for' evaluation rather than claiming it 'is suitable for' evaluation. (3) Analyze transformation rule productivity distribution (Table 1)—explain why dropping conjunction is only 2.0% while mixing dependents is 26.8%. Is this linguistic rarity or procedural limitation? (4) Quantify dependency parsing quality—report parsing accuracy on a sample of sentences and analyze how parsing errors propagate to transformed sentences. (5) Provide SICK inter-annotator agreement scores for comparison—contextualize what 'satisfactory' agreement means relative to SICK and other semantic datasets. (6) Analyze linguistic phenomenon coverage—which syntactic/semantic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented? Compare to SICK if possible. (7) Provide empirical evidence for two-stage annotation improvement—compare inter-annotator agreement for pairs with vs. without leader verification, or conduct controlled experiment. (8) Clarify post-correction procedure—specify systematic criteria for accepting/rejecting suggestions and analyze impact on semantic content. (9) Analyze bidirectional annotation effects—compare agreement for (a,b) vs. (b,a) pairs to assess whether bidirectionality inflates apparent agreement. (10) Analyze the 20 pairs with no majority entailment label (X)—explain why they lack consensus and how they should be handled. human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper presents a Polish evaluation dataset (10K sentence pairs) for compositional distributional semantics models, adapting the SICK corpus methodology to account for morphological complexity, free word order, and resource scarcity. The core contribution is systematic documentation of how SICK's image-based description and transformation-based expansion methodology can be adapted to a morphologically rich, under-resourced language through seven linguistically motivated transformation rules, a two-stage annotation procedure with leader judge verification, and bidirectional entailment annotation. The paper reports inter-annotator agreement of κ=0.732 (Fleiss' kappa for entailment) and α=0.780 (Krippendorff's alpha for relatedness), claiming these metrics indicate dataset suitability for Polish CDS model evaluation. The resource addresses a genuine gap in NLP infrastructure for under-resourced languages and is promised for public release. However, critical claims lack empirical validation: the dataset has not been used to evaluate actual Polish CDS models; the two-stage annotation procedure is presented as improving quality without empirical comparison to single-stage annotation; generalizability to other fusional languages is claimed without cross-linguistic testing; and comparability to SICK is asserted without formal comparison of dataset characteristics. The paper's strengths lie in practical resource contribution, transparent methodology documentation, and linguistically principled transformation rules. Its weaknesses lie in unsupported generalizability claims, missing benchmarking to SICK, and lack of empirical validation of core assertions.
strengths: Addresses genuine resource gap: The paper tackles a real and underexplored problem—the lack of evaluation datasets for CDS models in morphologically rich, under-resourced languages like Polish. This addresses a practical bottleneck in NLP model development for non-English languages.

Systematic and reproducible documentation: Sections 2–3 provide detailed, step-by-step procedures for image selection, transformation rules, pairing procedures, and annotation protocols. This level of documentation enables reproducibility and provides a template for other languages.

Linguistically principled transformation rules: The seven transformation rules are grounded in Polish morphosyntactic properties (fusional morphology, free word order, participle constructions) and demonstrate linguistic sophistication. Rules are not arbitrary but motivated by language-specific phenomena.

Reasonable inter-annotator agreement metrics: κ=0.732 for entailment and α=0.780 for relatedness are in a reasonable range for semantic annotation tasks. The choice of Krippendorff's alpha for ordinal relatedness scores is methodologically sound.

Pragmatic quality control: The two-stage annotation procedure with leader judge verification is a reasonable approach to mitigating errors in automatically transformed sentences. Post-correction process (228 punctuation fixes, 141 significant modifications) demonstrates attention to data quality.

Transparent acknowledgment of limitations: The paper explicitly documents deviations from SICK methodology and acknowledges limitations (imperfect dependency parsing, uneven transformation productivity). This transparency supports reproducibility and enables assessment of adaptation necessity.

Linguistically principled bidirectional annotation: The decision to annotate each pair in both directions (a,b) and (b,a) appropriately reflects the non-symmetric nature of entailment relations, demonstrating linguistic sophistication.

Practical resource contribution: The 10K-pair Polish dataset with human annotations for relatedness and entailment is a substantial resource that will enable future CDS model development for Polish. Public release commitment enhances value.
limitations: Lack of empirical validation through actual CDS model evaluation: The paper claims the dataset is 'suitable for evaluating Polish CDS models' but provides no evidence of actual model evaluation. Suitability is inferred from inter-annotator agreement metrics rather than demonstrated through downstream use. This is a critical gap between claimed utility and demonstrated utility.

Dependency parsing quality not quantified: The paper acknowledges transformations are 'fully automatic and to a certain extent based on imperfect dependency parsing' but does not quantify parsing error rates, types of errors, or their propagation to transformed sentences. This is critical because parsing errors directly affect transformation quality and dataset reliability.

Uneven transformation rule productivity without explanation: Table 1 shows productivity ranging from 2.0% (dropping conjunction) to 26.8% (mixing dependents)—a 13-fold variation. The paper does not explain whether underrepresented rules are linguistically rare in Polish or procedurally limited by the image-based methodology. This raises questions about rule completeness and dataset representativeness.

No empirical comparison of two-stage annotation to single-stage baseline: The paper claims two-stage annotation 'improves dataset quality for morphologically complex languages' but provides no empirical comparison. No quantification of error rates before/after leader judge verification, and no inter-annotator agreement analysis between leader judges and other judges.

Generalizability claims unsupported by empirical evidence: The paper claims the procedure 'can be adapted to non-English languages with significant linguistic differences' and is 'potentially applicable to other fusional languages,' but only Polish is demonstrated. No cross-linguistic testing or analysis of which aspects are Polish-specific vs. generalizable.

Comparability to SICK not formally demonstrated: The paper repeatedly claims the Polish dataset is 'comparable to the SICK corpus' but provides no formal comparison of inter-annotator agreement scores, label distributions, linguistic phenomenon coverage, or transformation rule effectiveness. What constitutes 'comparable' is not defined.

No analysis of linguistic phenomenon coverage: The paper does not analyze which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented in the dataset. Image-based descriptions may have systematic biases (e.g., overrepresentation of action verbs, underrepresentation of abstract concepts) that affect dataset utility for CDS evaluation.

Post-correction procedure appears ad-hoc: Section 3.3 describes post-corrections (228 punctuation/typo fixes, 141 significant modifications) but does not specify systematic criteria for accepting/rejecting suggestions or analyze whether corrections changed semantic content. The process appears ad-hoc without documented validation criteria.
open_questions: What is the dependency parsing accuracy on the image description corpus, and how many transformed sentences contain parsing-induced errors? The paper acknowledges imperfect parsing but does not quantify its impact. This is critical for assessing dataset reliability.

Why does transformation rule productivity vary so dramatically (2.0% to 26.8%)? Is dropping conjunction genuinely rare in Polish image descriptions, or is the transformation rule poorly specified? Does this distribution reflect linguistic properties or procedural limitations?
Has the dataset been used to evaluate actual Polish CDS models, and if so, what are the results? If not, what evidence would constitute demonstration of suitability for CDS model evaluation?

How do inter-annotator agreement metrics for the Polish dataset compare to SICK corpus agreement scores? What constitutes 'satisfactory' agreement for semantic tasks, and how does the Polish dataset compare to field standards?

Does the two-stage annotation procedure demonstrably improve quality relative to single-stage annotation? What is the error detection rate for leader judges, and does verification actually improve downstream annotation quality?

Which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented in the dataset? How does phenomenon coverage compare to SICK? Are image-based descriptions adequate for comprehensive CDS evaluation?

Is the procedure generalizable to other morphologically rich languages (Hungarian, Finnish, Czech), or are the seven transformation rules Polish-specific? What aspects of the procedure are language-general vs. language-specific?

Does bidirectional annotation inflate apparent agreement for entailment? Are annotators treating (a,b) and (b,a) as independent decisions or related decisions? Is agreement symmetric across directions?

What is the annotation pattern for the 20 pairs with no majority entailment label (X)? Do they represent genuine semantic ambiguity or annotation errors? How should they be handled in CDS model evaluation?
What systematic criteria were used to accept/reject annotator suggestions in the post-correction process? Did corrections change semantic content of sentences? How were modified pairs re-annotated?

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper presents a Polish evaluation dataset (10K sentence pairs) for compositional distributional semantics models, adapting the SICK corpus methodology to account for morphological complexity, free word order, and resource scarcity. The core contribution is systematic documentation of how SICK's image-based description and transformation-based expansion methodology can be adapted to a morphologically rich, under-resourced language through seven linguistically motivated transformation rules, a two-stage annotation procedure with leader judge verification, and bidirectional entailment annotation. The paper reports inter-annotator agreement of κ=0.732 (Fleiss' kappa for entailment) and α=0.780 (Krippendorff's alpha for relatedness), claiming these metrics indicate dataset suitability for Polish CDS model evaluation. The resource addresses a genuine gap in NLP infrastructure for under-resourced languages and is promised for public release.

Strengths:
- Addresses genuine resource gap: The paper tackles a real and underexplored problem—the lack of evaluation datasets for CDS models in morphologically rich, under-resourced languages like Polish.
- Systematic and reproducible documentation: Sections 2–3 provide detailed, step-by-step procedures for image selection, transformation rules, pairing procedures, and annotation protocols.
- Linguistically principled transformation rules: The seven transformation rules are grounded in Polish morphosyntactic properties (fusional morphology, free word order, participle constructions) and demonstrate linguistic sophistication.
- Reasonable inter-annotator agreement metrics: κ=0.732 for entailment and α=0.780 for relatedness are in a reasonable range for semantic annotation tasks.
- Pragmatic quality control: The two-stage annotation procedure with leader judge verification is a reasonable approach to mitigating errors in automatically transformed sentences.
- Transparent acknowledgment of limitations: The paper explicitly documents deviations from SICK methodology and acknowledges limitations (imperfect dependency parsing, uneven transformation productivity).
- Linguistically principled bidirectional annotation: The decision to annotate each pair in both directions (a,b) and (b,a) appropriately reflects the non-symmetric nature of entailment relations.
- Practical resource contribution: The 10K-pair Polish dataset with human annotations for relatedness and entailment is a substantial resource that will enable future CDS model development for Polish.

Limitations:
- Lack of empirical validation through actual CDS model evaluation: The paper claims the dataset is 'suitable for evaluating Polish CDS models' but provides no evidence of actual model evaluation. Suitability is inferred from inter-annotator agreement metrics rather than demonstrated through downstream use. This is a critical gap between claimed utility and demonstrated utility.
- Dependency parsing quality not quantified: The paper acknowledges transformations are 'fully automatic and to a certain extent based on imperfect dependency parsing' but does not quantify parsing error rates, types of errors, or their propagation to transformed sentences. This is critical because parsing errors directly affect transformation quality and dataset reliability.
- Uneven transformation rule productivity without explanation: Table 1 shows productivity ranging from 2.0% (dropping conjunction) to 26.8% (mixing dependents)—a 13-fold variation. The paper does not explain whether underrepresented rules are linguistically rare in Polish or procedurally limited by the image-based methodology. This raises questions about rule completeness and dataset representativeness.
- No empirical comparison of two-stage annotation to single-stage baseline: The paper claims two-stage annotation 'improves dataset quality for morphologically complex languages' but provides no empirical comparison. No quantification of error rates before/after leader judge verification, and no inter-annotator agreement analysis between leader judges and other judges.
- Generalizability claims unsupported by empirical evidence: The paper claims the procedure 'can be adapted to non-English languages with significant linguistic differences' and is 'potentially applicable to other fusional languages,' but only Polish is demonstrated. No cross-linguistic testing or analysis of which aspects are Polish-specific vs. generalizable.
- Comparability to SICK not formally demonstrated: The paper repeatedly claims the Polish dataset is 'comparable to the SICK corpus' but provides no formal comparison of inter-annotator agreement scores, label distributions, linguistic phenomenon coverage, or transformation rule effectiveness. What constitutes 'comparable' is not defined.
- No analysis of linguistic phenomenon coverage: The paper does not analyze which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented in the dataset. Image-based descriptions may have systematic biases (e.g., overrepresentation of action verbs, underrepresentation of abstract concepts) that affect dataset utility for CDS evaluation.
- Post-correction procedure appears ad-hoc: Section 3.3 describes post-corrections (228 punctuation/typo fixes, 141 significant modifications) but does not specify systematic criteria for accepting/rejecting suggestions or analyze whether corrections changed semantic content. The process appears ad-hoc without documented validation criteria.

Open Questions:
- What is the dependency parsing accuracy on the image description corpus, and how many transformed sentences contain parsing-induced errors? The paper acknowledges imperfect parsing but does not quantify its impact. This is critical for assessing dataset reliability.
- Why does transformation rule productivity vary so dramatically (2.0% to 26.8%)? Is dropping conjunction genuinely rare in Polish image descriptions, or is the transformation rule poorly specified? Does this distribution reflect linguistic properties or procedural limitations?
- Has the dataset been used to evaluate actual Polish CDS models, and if so, what are the results? If not, what evidence would constitute demonstration of suitability for CDS model evaluation?
- How do inter-annotator agreement metrics for the Polish dataset compare to SICK corpus agreement scores? What constitutes 'satisfactory' agreement for semantic tasks, and how does the Polish dataset compare to field standards?
- Does the two-stage annotation procedure demonstrably improve quality relative to single-stage annotation? What is the error detection rate for leader judges, and does verification actually improve downstream annotation quality?
- Which linguistic phenomena are well-represented vs. underrepresented in the dataset? How does phenomenon coverage compare to SICK? Are image-based descriptions adequate for comprehensive CDS evaluation?
- Is the procedure generalizable to other morphologically rich languages (Hungarian, Finnish, Czech), or are the seven transformation rules Polish-specific? What aspects of the procedure are language-general vs. language-specific?
- Does bidirectional annotation inflate apparent agreement for entailment? Are annotators treating (a,b) and (b,a) as independent decisions or related decisions? Is agreement symmetric across directions?
- What is the annotation pattern for the 20 pairs with no majority entailment label (X)? Do they represent genuine semantic ambiguity or annotation errors? How should they be handled in CDS model evaluation?

Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.
